title: Delegate clearly, keep a healthy pace, review every week

say: Delegate clearly, keep a healthy pace, and review every week.
This is the video for Module 3 of Productivity and Time Management at Work.
A good system must work week after week without wearing you out. Delegation means handing a task to someone else while you stay responsible for the result.

say: Then you learn to protect your pace, and to run a weekly review that shows whether your methods work.

say: Delegate tasks that repeat and that someone else can learn. Keep decisions that need your authority.
Then write a brief. First, the outcome. A reorder list in the shared sheet is clearer than, check the stock.
Give a deadline, with a date and time.
Share the resources: files, templates, or past examples.
Say what they can decide alone, and what needs your approval. Move them up as trust grows.
And agree when you will check in, so it feels normal, not like suspicion.
Most failed delegation is a briefing problem, so put it in writing. And never delegate access to your bank app, PINs or passwords.

panel.heading: A five-point delegation brief
panel.rule: Most failed delegation is a briefing problem. Write it down.

say: Esther spends about 3 hours every Saturday on stock. She writes Kunle a brief on WhatsApp, with the outcome, a deadline, the sheet template, and the rule that she approves and pays.
Week 1 they count together. Then Kunle counts alone, and Esther checks 10 items at random. Two errors in week 2, none in week 3.
In week 4 he recommends, and she decides. She saves about 2.5 hours a week for building relationships with two nearby schools.
The World Health Organization describes burn-out as resulting from chronic workplace stress that has not been managed. It has three dimensions. First, exhaustion.

cards.d: Your energy is used up. Rest at the weekend no longer restores you.
Negative or cynical about your job. You stop caring about work that used to matter.
You accomplish less, even when you work longer.

say: Second, mental distance from your job, or feeling negative about it.

cards.d: Your energy is used up. Rest at the weekend no longer restores you.
Negative or cynical about your job. You stop caring about work that used to matter.
You accomplish less, even when you work longer.

say: Third, feeling less effective. And here is the trap. Working more hours to catch up often feeds the cycle.

say: End each workday with 10 minutes to capture loose ends, check tomorrow, and choose the first task. Then stop.
When a new request arrives and your week is full, ask which task should give way, rather than silently adding hours.
Take a real lunch break, and plan your leave early.
Sleep, regular meals, water and some movement are what attention runs on.

If exhaustion, low mood, poor sleep or loss of interest continue for weeks, speak to a doctor or a qualified counsellor, and to HR if you have one. If you ever feel unable to cope, contact a health professional immediately and tell someone you trust.

panel.heading: Practical protections
panel.rule: If it lasts for weeks, speak to a doctor or qualified counsellor

say: Adaeze completed only 2 of her 5 priorities last week, and she feels drained every morning.
She lists her commitments with hours. 46 hours of work, against about 32 hours of real capacity.

say: She brings options, not complaints. I suggest these two changes. Which would you prefer? They delegate reconciliations and move one audit deadline.
Within three weeks she leaves by 6 most days, and completes 4 of 5 priorities.

say: Systems decay. So block a fixed weekly slot, like Friday afternoon. First, get clear. Empty your capture inbox and saved messages.

panel.heading: Get clear, get current, get creative

say: Get current. Tick off finished actions, follow up anything overdue on Waiting for, and check your calendar.

say: Get creative. Look at your OKR. Is there a new idea or risk to act on?

say: Then choose next week's top three priorities, and block time for them before the week fills up.

say: Each week she records priorities finished, focused hours, interruptions, and her energy from 1 to 5. And she changes only one thing each week, so she can see what helped.
Week 1, just 6 focused hours. She had planned three large reports, so she broke them into sections. By week 4, 10 focused hours.
Interruptions fell from 15 to 7 a day after she muted the staff group chat. Now she has numbers to show her manager.
To remember. Delegate with a written brief, and track it on Waiting for. More hours often feeds burnout, so use a shutdown routine. Review every week, and change one thing at a time.
